Ep 214 Holiday Gift Guide for Architects 2026

November 15, 2026 by Bob Borson 3 Comments

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 20:27
Instaread

Seventeen years of gift guides, and as I sit here rubbing my temples, I am starting to think I should have picked something easier to do every November. Architects remain painfully particular, and apparently “I already have one, but I like this one better” is still a perfectly reasonable justification for wanting another desk lamp. Andrew and I have once again spent far too much time deciding what you should buy for someone who will immediately ask if you kept the receipt. Welcome to Episode 214: The 2026 Life of an Architect Holiday Gift Guide.

[Note: If you are reading this via email, click here to access the on-site audio player]

Podcast: Embed

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | Android | iHeartRadio | TuneIn


Today we find ourselves back on familiar ground – 17 years’ worth of familiar ground. Just like last year, and every year since 2010, we are here to help all the befuddled gift-givers by telling you what to buy your architect loved one, with the understanding that you can blame Andrew and me if they don’t like the gift.

Disclosure: We only recommend products that we would use ourselves and all opinions expressed here are our own. This post may contain affiliate links that add no additional cost to you and a small commission may be earned. These commissions go towards paying the operational costs associated with ‘Life of an Architect’. Please consider using them as a way of supporting the content on this site. This disclosure is in accordance with the Federal Trade Commission’s 16 CFR, Part 255: “Guides Concerning the Use of Endorsements and Testimonials in Advertising.”

Round 1 jump to 08:00

Keenray Luxury Towel Warmer – $102

Bob: I spend a fair amount of time thinking about what makes a bathroom better, and apparently one answer is a bucket that heats your towels. The Keenray towel warmer holds two over-sized bath towels, operates with a single button, and shuts itself off automatically, which is about the level of responsibility I want from a bathroom appliance. You can also use it for bathrobes and pajamas, should you decide that room temperature is no longer meeting your standards. This is the sort of gift that feels slightly ridiculous until you step out of the shower and wrap yourself in a warm towel … then you start wondering why everyone else isn’t willing to live like this?!

My daughter gave me this gift 2 years ago – I love it and highly endorse adding it to your bathroom (along with the sense of superiority that comes along with it for free).

 

Lamy 2000 Fountain Pen  –  $279

Andrew: I have become a fairly avid pen collector. Some pens, I will admit, I purchase for my “collection,” while others I purchase for daily use. I like to use fountain pens as my daily instrument these days, mainly because they make me slow down a bit when I use them. They require me to be more deliberate and mindful of the marks I am making. While this may seem like something a bit “too extra”, I find it increasingly important to the way I communicate with others. This fountain pen has been on my list for a while, and I recently was able to acquire one. I will admit my recent purchase was based on a nice discount code I had, which let me save significantly off the retail price. But as far as pens go, even at normal price, it is not an outrageous price for a premium fountain pen. I know it seems like it would be, but some pens cost thousands; just see my choice from last year (still a dream pen).  As an alternative, I would offer the Pelikan P40 Pura.

Round 2 jump to 15:23

Weck 745 One-Liter Tulip Jars – $15

Bob: I realize that putting a glass jar on a gift guide requires some explanation, but architects have been getting excited about well-proportioned containers for a very long time. The Weck 745 Tulip Jar holds one liter, or roughly 34 ounces, and pairs a curved glass body with a wide opening, glass lid, rubber sealing ring, and removable steel clips. The jar is dishwasher safe, and the wide mouth makes filling and cleaning it considerably less irritating than either task needs to be. Use it for coffee, cookies, homemade preserves, or whatever currently occupies a plastic container you would prefer nobody noticed. I like that you can see how the whole thing works, right down to the clips holding the lid in place. Apparently, even my food storage needs an expressed structural system.

I also have these and personally recommend them – it doesn’t matter if you don’t want to maintain your own sourdough starter – there are other awesome uses.

Steeping vodka in pineapple? Check.
Organizing your pens and pencils? Check
Did I say steeping vodka in pineapple?

Western Digital External Hard Drive  –  $500 for 16 TB (various sizes available)

Andrew: I have lots of files. Lots of large files. I started using these larger external storage drives when I was still running my practice, as a layer of redundancy. At that time, I also used them for my smaller-scale home/personal files. But now, in the years since, my personal file storage needs have become quite large as well. I have all of my digital photos and videos from family, travels, and the like. Those continue to increase in size and number, especially from my daughters’ time in sports. Also, while it may make me more of an “old-timer”, I still own music except a vast majority of it is digital. So I have lots of music files. Then there is all the digital movies I own as well. So my digital entertainment media footprint is always growing. I have my teaching files (work) as well. I also keep a large amount of my students’ work for various purposes. Lastly, I have all of my own personal documents and such. So my complete digital footprint is a bit unruly. So, I’m about to double my capacity with this device. I have had the 8TB version of this for about 8 years and have not had a single glitch. Now, I plan to simply upgrade. I find it to be very useful. Like I say in the episode, I could grab this on my way out of my burning house and have saved almost everything I need. That is not 100% true, but about 80% at least.

Round 3 jump to 25:53

Turtlebox Ranger Bluetooth Speaker – $250

Bob: The Turtlebox Ranger looks like something that belongs in a toolbox, which is part of the appeal. This portable Bluetooth speaker weighs 2.4 pounds, delivers up to 105 decibels, and has an IP67 waterproof and dust-proof rating, meaning it can survive considerably more outdoor activity than I typically volunteer to experience. Turtlebox advertises more than 12 hours of battery life, depending on volume, and the built-in magnetic side mounts let you attach it to a compatible metal surface rather than sacrifice valuable space next to your drink. You can also pair two for stereo sound or connect multiple compatible Turtlebox speakers through Party Mode, should your music need its own infrastructure. I like a speaker that can spend the afternoon beside the smoker without requiring me to monitor the weather while allowing my neighbors to enjoy my taste in music … whether the neighbors share that enthusiasm probably depends on the playlist.

 

GMKTek M6 Ultra Gaming Mini PC  –  $680  (other models available)

Andrew: This one is purely about setting up a system for AI Agentic work. This unit contains everything you need to operate as an independent computer. Essentially, it is a laptop with no screen. It is marketed as a gaming mini-PC, so it has everything you need to operate as an independent computer. This one has pretty good specs, mainly because I need the large storage capacity. Setting up this machine as an Isolated system to house and run AI work keeps all of your “private data” private. I have been working in various ways with AI systems, and of course, as with most people, these are public systems. So, this little computer attempts to generate a bit more privacy for the information and data I use within these public systems. As I move into more agentic work, I want to make sure I can protect my information and knowledge from the public realm. I know this may not be something everyone using AI is required to utilize, but as you become more involved and work in depth, this type of security and separation becomes more important.

Round 4 jump to 32:45

Stelton 014 Stainless Steel Serving Tray – $299

Waterford Aras Decanter Round – $415

Waterford 6oz Straight Tumbler (set of 2) $170

Bob: I am counting this as one gift idea because it all sits on the same tray, which seems like a perfectly reasonable accounting practice. The foundation is the Stelton AJ serving tray, designed by Arne Jacobsen as part of the Cylinda-line collection. Made from stainless steel and measuring approximately 13.2 inches in diameter, it has a low rim and handles that follow the circular geometry rather than interrupt it. This is the sort of detail that makes architects disproportionately happy. It also gives a decanter and a pair of glasses a designated home, which helps distinguish a considered arrangement from several things you left on the counter.

The Waterford Aras round decanter ($415) and matching straight tumblers ($170 for two) finish the setup with some weight and a little sparkle. The decanter stands 10.2 inches tall, while the glasses are a relatively restrained 6 ounces each, measuring 2.8 inches across and 3.1 inches high. I like the pairing of the simple steel tray with the vertical cuts in the crystal, a pattern Waterford says was inspired by the turrets of Irish castles. Apparently, I can find an architectural justification for drinking bourbon. Any of these pieces would make a good gift individually, but together they suggest that the recipient has reached a point in life where the presentation deserves as much consideration as the contents.

Walker Slater, Edward Shetland Tweed Jacket  –  $440  

Andrew:  I certainly know this one appeals to only a select few out there. But as this list is about what I want/need this year, this one is on my list. I have been in need of a new sport coat for a few years, actually. But I have never been able to find a coat that seems “just right.” So now I think I may have found it. This company was founded in 1989 and is located in Scotland. They pride themselves on their “hard-wearing classic clothing for the Scottish Highlands.” They work specifically with tweeds and take great pride in their clothing craftsmanship. While I do not yet own this coat, it appears to meet my specific needs. This is a twill fabric with some texture, and it does not look like the jacket portion of a three-piece suit. It is structured a bit differently and has a more casual look. This is not to say it cannot look dressier, but it fills that space where I like most of my wardrobe: somewhere between casual and dressy. I know many might call it “business casual”, but I dislike that term so much. Yet, I am certain this coat fits that bill. This is on the higher end of what I might want the price range to be; it is also a coat that will last and not go out of style, since it has a classic fit and cut. While $450 might feel expensive, this coat should last a long time in your wardrobe. For me, of course, it will be all black, and that is as timeless as it gets.

Round 5 jump to 40:41

Rabbit W6004N Lever Action Corkscrew Opener – $59

Bob: Opening a bottle of wine in front of other people is a poor time to discover that your corkscrew requires better technique than you possess. The Rabbit Original Lever Corkscrew takes most of that opportunity for embarrassment out of the process, using a pair of gripping handles and a lever mechanism to pull the cork with minimal effort. This version comes with a foil cutter and an extra nonstick spiral, and its metal, nylon, and polycarbonate construction gives it the appearance of a tool with a specific job … and I appreciate that. There are smaller corkscrews that fit neatly in a pocket, but I am opening wine in my kitchen, not trying to sneak equipment onto a submarine. Give this to someone with a good bottle and you have handled both the gift and the immediate plans for using it.

 

Gotrax R7 20” (Ranger 20) E-Bike – $900  

Andrew: This one is just for pure fun. I will admit it is not really a practical gift, or even one about exercise or fitness. It is solely about fun and zipping around the neighborhood or to my campus for work. My daily commute is less than three miles and could be made on this e-bike when the weather allows, at about the same speed as my car. But this would be much more fun, in my opinion. I know this isn’t for everyone, and some may find them a nuisance in their areas. I would agree; they are a nuisance when operated by inconsiderate riders. I know there are many, but as a person who also used to ride a normal bike, I ride with respect to the law and regulations of the road, not like a selfish maniac who thinks they always have the right of way no matter the situation.  There is also a less expensive version with a smaller motor. I chose this one due to my own physical stature, which would probably benefit from a larger wattage motor. So my advice here: ride responsibly and have fun! (smaller motor version $700)

Round 6 jump to 48:05

Huepar Laser Level – $100
Huepar 12’ Laser Level pole – $90

Bob: Architects can spot a crooked picture from across a room and then spend the rest of the evening trying to decide whether they can straighten it without making things awkward. We spend our working lives aligning things, and apparently that particular switch does not turn off when we go home. The Huepar B03CG laser level supports this annoying pursuit of perfection by projecting three complete 360-degree green laser planes, one horizontal and two vertical, for aligning frames, shelves, tile, or anything else whose placement might otherwise bother you indefinitely. It is self-leveling and comes with a rechargeable lithium battery, USB-C power cord, magnetic pivoting base, and hard carrying case. Establishing a consistent reference across an entire room makes it easier to get those relationships right, even if you are the only person who would have noticed they were wrong.

The companion Huepar LP36A telescoping pole makes the laser easier to position at the height you actually need, rather than whatever height you can achieve with a stack of books on a dining chair. It extends to approximately 12 feet and includes a tripod, adjustable mounting bracket, carrying bag, and both 1/4-inch and 5/8-inch mounting options. There is also a feature that allows you to pressure-fit the pole between two horizontal surfaces (like the floor and the ceiling). This is why I would put the two together as a gift: the laser establishes the reference, and the pole keeps the setup from becoming its own project. You still have to decide where the pictures belong, which, speaking from experience, can take considerably longer than hanging them.

Nikon Z fc Retro -inspired Compact Mirrorless Digital Camera – $1000   

Andrew:  I already have a DSLR camera set with several lenses. While it does take excellent photos, it is bulky and not very convenient to carry around and use. It works for specific conditions, but on the go, it is not really one of those. So that is where this camera comes into the picture. (pun!) This is a mirrorless digital camera with the same photographic quality as a DSLR, but with a much smaller footprint and weight. These cameras are fairly new technology, so they are a bit more expensive than a small digital camera, but they rival DSLRs in operation and photo quality. This model, like most major brands, also lets you use the same lenses from your DSLR setup. So you can swap lenses to meet your needs. As you can see in the image, this camera is barely larger than the lens, which makes it more portable. I can fit this type of camera in my jacket pocket or small bag. This specific version is “retro-styled” so that it looks more like an old SLR camera from the 70s or 80s. I like that feature. But if you don’t, they also make a non-retro version. The one I have shown/priced is the body plus one lens, but you can also get the body-only version if you don’t need to add another lens to your kit.

Architecture Books

We always have books on our list because of all the possible “I don’t know what to get, hope you like this”, books are the easiest thing to get. Andrew and I each maintain our own lists, stored offsite for easy upkeep and rotation. A visual selection is shown here, but there are more if you click on the links or the individual images.

Bob’s Books

I have more architecture books than I can reasonably justify, and somehow that has done very little to slow my interest in acquiring more. The unfortunate side effect is that a growing library provides an increasingly thorough record of all the things other architects have figured out that I apparently have not. What begins as inspiration can turn into a fairly comprehensive assessment of my own shortcomings if I spend too much time looking at the drawings …  but I keep buying the books anyway, partly because I still have things to learn and partly because I would rather be inspired and slightly demoralized than convinced I already know enough.

 


Andrew’s Books
This year again I have an updated list of Architecture books. I do have a list for the Year of 2026 like years past. There are a few specific wants on that list for me. While I did add to my library in 2026, many of those books were not first published in 2026. So this year was more about filling gaps or finding new “old books” that better suited my current interests or specific architects. This list offers a wide array of books for anyone who enjoys architecture, likes pretty images, or even needs some technical inspiration or support. As architects, we rely on a vast amount of information to do our work and keep us inspired. The list is a wide array of monographs, technical books, and theory about architecture and the built world. I find that now I am more interested not only in the making of buildings, but also in the ideas behind them or the conditions that generated them. For me, that still means good old-fashioned hard copy books. I never seem to grow tired of adding to my library, but I am running out of room.

Ep 214: Holiday Gift Guide for Architects

Ho-Ho-Ho and we are done! If you somehow make it through these picks without finding a single thing worth wrapping, the archives are waiting below. Years of gift guides, all vetted, all field-tested, and none of them built from the same recycled lists that show up everywhere else. There is plenty in the mix that an actual architect would want, which feels like a small holiday miracle on its own.
